scenes.name: Siouxsie and the Banshees
scenes.book: Postpunk. Romper todo y empezar de nuevo
scenes.author: Simon Reynolds
scenes.desc: Fans de Roxy Music que no creían en el igualitarismo punk («No todo el mundo puede hacerlo»): minimalismo por descarte (sin solos, sin finales de batería), guitarra con flanger entre la Velvet y la ducha de Psicosis, la voz gélida de Siouxsie y letras antisentimentales sobre la locura y los suburbios («Suburban Relapse», «Jigsaw Feeling»). The Scream (1978), Join Hands («Icon», el padrenuestro), Kaleidoscope con John McGeoch y Budgie, Juju (1981), su obra cumbre y matriz del gótico (magia, vudú, Halloween), y A Kiss in the Dreamhouse (1982), decadencia fin de siglo y psicodelia inglesa. Siouxsie quería ser «un palo en la rueda de la mediocridad».

scenes.name: Gótico
scenes.book: Postpunk. Romper todo y empezar de nuevo
scenes.author: Simon Reynolds
scenes.desc: Término que Hannett aplicó a Joy Division y luego insulto para los epígonos, hasta que en 1982 los fans lo adoptan como estandarte frente a la excesiva luminosidad del new pop: glamour sepulcral, retorno de lo reprimido, emociones atemporales. Bauhaus («Bela Lugosi's Dead», 1979, el comienzo propiamente dicho; Peter Murphy, sex symbol heredero de Adam Ant y Bowie), The Birthday Party (el gótico americano de Nick Cave: «Release the Bats», Junkyard), Killing Joke («música de tensión», del funk de PiL a Black Sabbath, con un aura inquietante), The Cure (gótico light: Seventeen Seconds, Faith, Pornography). El club The Batcave (1982), el «positive punk», Southern Death Cult, Theatre of Hate, The Sisters of Mercy («¡Nosotros sí somos una banda de rock!»), el death rock de Los Ángeles y Kukl con Björk. Su deriva: coqueteos totalitarios y la conversión en versión postpunk del heavy metal (The Cult).

podcast.title: Denial of Goth Affiliation
podcast.body: Robert Smith later disavowed The Cure's Goth label, claiming it was a "big misunderstanding" and that they were never truly a Goth band. "And Robert Smith would later claim that the cure were never really Goth in the first place."

podcast.title: Email Communication Habits
podcast.body: Robert Smith of The Cure has a distinct habit of responding to emails entirely in capital letters, which is simply his preferred style and not an indication of yelling. He also limits his email interactions to only reading and responding on Thursdays. "He's not yelling at you. That's just how he does things."

podcast.title: Essential to Goth Scene
podcast.body: Robert Smith is considered essential to the Goth scene, as the scene probably wouldn't be what it is today without his influence, regardless of whether he acknowledges the Goth classification. "But let's face it, the Goths seem probably would not be what it is today without Robert Smith, whether he wants to admit it or not."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Influence of Electric Warrior
podcast.body: As a young artist, Robert Smith was "completely besotted" by T-Rex's *Electric Warrior* album and Mark Bowen, an influence shared with his future bandmate, Lol Tolhurst. "A young Robert Smith, who would later from the cure, was completely besotted by Electric Warrior and Mark Bowen."

podcast.title: Praise for "Loveless"
podcast.body: Robert Smith of The Cure expressed profound admiration for My Bloody Valentine's "Loveless," stating that it "pissed on all current music, including his own," and ranked it among his top three albums of all time. "Robert Smith, de De Keehr, dijo de él, que se meaba en toda la música del momento, incluida la suya, y que está entre sus tres discos preferidos de la historia."

xref.title: Robert Smith's "The Hair" and Controversial Haircut (Late 1986)
xref.body: As one of the biggest bands from the early 1980s Goth/Dark Stuff scene, The Cure's look, particularly Robert Smith's signature "The Hair"—a long, unruly mop of jet-black hair—was widely emulated. "The Hair" first appeared around 1982 with `Pornography` and peaked in "spiderweb" style around 1984, but its sudden disappearance in late 1986 when Smith got a military-style haircut provoked a swift and angry reaction from fans, reminiscent of the outrage when Elvis Presley cut his hair for the army in 1957. Smith subsequently learned his lesson and began growing it out again, with the iconic style returning to normal by 1992. "The day Robert Smith lost the hair, and angered cure fans around the world."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Apology and Resolution
xref.body: In 2019, Morrissey issued an apology for his "terrible things" said about Robert Smith 35 years prior, claiming he "didn't mean them" and jokingly attributing it to Tourette's syndrome (which he does not have). Smith accepted the apology, noting the feud had long faded from his consciousness. "In 2019, Morrissey said, I said some terrible things about him 35 years ago, but I didn't mean them. It's great when you complain everything on Tourette's syndrome."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Consistency of Speaking and Singing Voice
xref.body: Robert Smith's speaking voice has been observed to be very similar in quality to his distinctive singing voice, a trait confirmed by individuals who have interviewed him. "And I can confirm that I've interviewed Robert on a number of occasions, and his speaking voices very similar in quality to his singing voice."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Distinctive Vocal Style
xref.body: Robert Smith's unselfconscious and quirky singing voice, though not universally appreciated initially, contributed to the growing diversity of vocal styles in the music scene. "And although Robert Smith's unselfconscious quirky singing voice was not appreciated by everyone, at least at first, it added to the increasing variety of voices that were being heard."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Forefront of British Goth (Despite Disavowal)
xref.body: The Cure, active since 1976, established themselves at the forefront of British Goth culture, even though they sometimes disavowed the label and were occasionally criticized for being too pop. Robert Smith remains a torchbearer for Goth regardless of his personal preference for the label. "The cure, who had been around since 1976, had established themselves at the forefront of British Goth culture, although they sometimes disavowed being Goths and were sometimes ostracized for being too pop."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Influence on Contemporary Artists
xref.body: The album *Loveless* had a profound and widespread impact, blowing away musicians such as Trent Reznor, Billy Corgan, Robert Smith, Courtney Love, and The Edge of U2. Its influence far exceeded its commercial sales, cementing its status as a seminal work in alternative music and being frequently cited by contemporary bands as an inspiration. "Everyone from Trent Resner to Billy Corgan to Robert Smith to Courtney Love to the edge of YouTube were blown away by what they heard on that album."

xref.title: Lineup Audition with Cult Hero
xref.body: In 1979, Robert Smith faced lineup issues, particularly regarding a bass player for The Cure. To thoroughly assess Simon Gallup as a potential fit, Smith orchestrated a "complete and full mock-up" in secret, forming the pseudonymous band Cult Hero to record a single with Gallup. This allowed Smith to confirm his compatibility with Gallup before officially bringing him into The Cure, alongside guitarist Paul Thompson, who had been in an earlier version of the band. "Robert found that he liked working with Simon, and guitarist Paul Thompson, who had been in an earlier version of the cure, was brought in, and now we have a new line up."

xref.body: Marilyn Manson uses Mac Cosmetics, making the brand a preferred choice among musicians known for their theatrical makeup. This association further solidified Mac Cosmetics' reputation within the alternative music scene. "Marilyn Manson's brand and it's also the choice of the Cures Robert Smith makeup brand."

xref.title: Marilyn Manson's Planned Fragrance and Cosmetics Line
xref.body: Marilyn Manson has expressed intentions to launch his own fragrance, possibly a perfume or toilet water, and subsequently a line of cosmetics. His interest in cosmetics is underscored by his status as one of MAC Cosmetics' best customers, a brand favored by performers like Manson and Robert Smith of The Cure for its durability under hot stage lights. "Manson wants to launch his own fragrance, a perfume or a toyler water or something."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Petty Feud with Morrissey (The Smiths)
xref.body: A perceived feud between Robert Smith and Morrissey began in the 1980s, largely perpetuated by the British music media. Morrissey reportedly called Smith a "Wingebag" in an interview, to which Smith retaliated by saying Morrissey was "so depressing that if he doesn't off himself soon, I probably will." Robert Smith later expressed regret for the "petty feud." "Morrissey appears to have started it off by calling Robert Smith a Wingebag in an interview. Smith retaliated in another interview saying that, Morrissey so depressing that if he doesn't off himself soon, I probably will."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Petty Feud with Robert Smith (The Cure)
xref.body: Morrissey initiated a perceived feud in the 1980s by calling Robert Smith a "Wingebag" in an interview, leading to retaliatory remarks from Smith. Morrissey later acknowledged the feud as "petty" and expressed regret. "Morrissey appears to have started it off by calling Robert Smith a Wingebag in an interview."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Resolved Conflict and Apology
xref.body: In 2019, Morrissey apologized for his past remarks, claiming they were made 35 years prior and he "didn't mean them," facetiously blaming Tourette's syndrome. Robert Smith responded that the apology was "slightly odd" as the feud had not been at the forefront of his mind for 20-30 years, and he never fully understood the problem to begin with, considering it far from important now. "In 2019, Morrissey said, I said some terrible things about him 35 years ago, but I didn't mean them. It's great when you complain everything on Tourette's syndrome."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Robert Smith's "The Hair"
xref.body: Robert Smith of The Cure is renowned for his signature, voluminous, unruly mass of jet black hair, colloquially known as "The Hair," a style that has been extensively imitated since the band began releasing records in the late 1970s. "Now that thing on top of Robert's head has simply become known as The Hair."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Robert Smith's Early Influences
xref.body: Robert Smith's older siblings introduced him to a diverse range of artists, including The Beatles, The Rolling Stones, Captain Beefheart, David Bowie, Jimi Hendrix, and Nick Drake. The subsequent arrival of punk rock, with bands like Sex Pistols, Ramones, and Elvis Costello, further shaped his musical direction and helped him find his artistic niche. "His older brother and sister had filled his head with beetles and stone songs, but they also subjected him to a lot of Captain B-Fart, and David Bowie, and Jimmy Hendrix and Nick Drake. And then when punk came along, it was Sex Pistols Ramones Elvis Costello. Young Robert found his niche."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Robert Smith's Goth Denial
xref.body: Robert Smith, the band's frontman, later stated that The Cure were never truly Goth and that their association with the genre was a "big misunderstanding." "And Robert Smith would later claim that the cure were never really Goth in the first place."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Robert Smith's Hair Maintenance (or Lack Thereof)
xref.body: Robert Smith described his iconic "The Hair" as naturally unruly, claiming it looks the same when he wakes up and that he often goes "a couple of months at a time" without combing it, resulting in a "haystacky vibe"; he also revealed his wife threatened to leave him if he ever shaved it again. "Honestly, I just get up and it's like this."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Robert Smith's Influences
xref.body: Robert Smith's musical upbringing was shaped by his older brother and sister, who introduced him to The Beatles and The Rolling Stones. They also exposed him to more unconventional artists like Captain Beefheart, David Bowie, Jimi Hendrix, and Nick Drake. The arrival of punk further influenced Smith, with bands like the Sex Pistols, Ramones, and Elvis Costello helping him discover his artistic niche. "His older brother and sister had filled his head with beetles and stone songs, but they also subjected him to a lot of Captain B. Fart, and David Bowie, and Jimmy Hendrix and Nick Drake."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Robert Smith's Mac Cosmetics Use
xref.body: Robert Smith, the front person of The Cure, is a proud user of Mac Cosmetics, noting a "nice symmetry" because he was called "Mac" when working on The Glove album seven years prior. He actively engages in "high-pitched makeup meetings" with the company, specifically advocating for the development of a good black eyeshadow, and has received makeup designed to remain intact even under extreme conditions. "The Cure featuring Robert Smith, proud purchaser of Mac cosmetics. ...I was mown in about the fact that my makeup was running when we last played in the desert and they've given me this makeup that they say, if I ever play on the surface of the sun, at least my makeup will remain intact even though the rest of me may burn. The only thing they're missing is a good black eyeshadow. I have to tell them and it's time I've over there in one of my makeup, my high-pitched makeup meetings I have with them nearly. It looks good. It's about seven years to call me Mac when we did the glove album. So there's a kind of a nice symmetry for me and actually ending up using makeup that seems to have my name on the front of it."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Robert Smith's Mid-1980s Haircut Controversy
xref.body: In the mid-1980s, Robert Smith cut his distinctive hair short, leading to such an intense negative reaction from his fanbase and strong disapproval from his wife that he has abstained from doing so again. "There was a time in the middle 1980s when Robert cut it all down, but fans freaked out so much and his wife disapproved so strongly that he's never done it again."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Robert Smith's Past Shaved Heads
xref.body: Robert Smith disclosed that he has shaved his head three times over a 20-year period, including once in the 1980s, despite ongoing opposition from his wife to any future similar changes. "Yeah, I've done it three times actually. I've shaved my head in the last 20 years."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Robert Smith's Preference for MAC Cosmetics
xref.body: Robert Smith of The Cure is noted as a loyal customer of MAC Cosmetics, a brand favored by performers like Marilyn Manson. This preference is attributed to MAC products' ability to hold up well under the hot lights of a stage. "A lot of performers like Manson and Robert Smith are the cure for Mac because it holds up nicely under hot stage lights."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Robert Smith's Vocal Philosophy
xref.body: Robert Smith, a tenor, has explored various singing styles throughout his career, including punk, a soft vocal approach, and his current "agonized lover" style, which incorporates yelping falsetto and occasional low growls. He does not consider himself a traditional singer, focusing instead on achieving the necessary emotional state for a song rather than technical perfection, and has deliberately varied his vocal approaches to avoid predictability. "In the early days, I never cared about giving a performance. I just worked myself up into the state of mind needed for the song, and that would be it. Some of the things I sang were pretty good, but a lot of it was out of tune. There was one point where I thought I was starting to get too predictable. So ever since then, I've tried to sing in different voices. I find it especially difficult to sing in a voice, which is far removed from the way I talk."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Robert Smith's Vocal Style and Self-Perception
xref.body: Robert Smith is a tenor who has experimented with various vocal styles, evolving from a punk period to a soft vocal approach, and eventually to an "agonized lover" persona characterized by yelping falsetto and occasional low growls. Smith does not view himself as a traditional singer, stating that in the early days, he focused more on achieving the necessary emotional state for a song, often resulting in out-of-tune performances. He consciously started singing in different voices to avoid predictability, finding it challenging to sing in a voice far from his natural speaking tone. "In the early days, I never cared about giving a performance. I just worked myself up into the state of mind needed for the song, and that would be it."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Simon Gallup's Tenure
xref.body: Simon Gallup joined The Cure as their second bass player in 1979. He was fired in 1982 after a fist fight with Robert Smith over a bar bill but rejoined two years later and has been with the band ever since. "He came on board in 1979 but then he was fired in 1982 when he got into a fist fight with Robert Smith over who was supposed to pay a bar bill."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: The Cure's "Job Application" Band
xref.body: Cult Hero was essentially The Cure performing under a pseudonym, specifically designed by Robert Smith as a way to test out new bassist Simon Gallup in 1979 without official commitment. Robert, Simon, Robert's two sisters, and other friends secretly recorded a single, "I'm a Cult Hero," with Robert's mailman, Frank Bell, on lead vocals to further conceal their identities. "That's essentially the cure trading as Cult Hero, with Robert Smith's postman on lead vocals."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
